input:
In this study, a comprehensive comparison was carried out between two different catalyst forms for the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to produce formaldehyde. The performance of each catalyst was evaluated in terms of space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), together with pressure drop and activity loss. All of the tests were conducted under identical conditions, namely at a temperature of 230 °C and a pressure of 60 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3, and it should be noted that only a single feed composition was utilised throughout the investigation.

The structured catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.74 kg L-1 h-1, accompanied by a pressure drop of just 0.15 bar, and it exhibited an activity loss of 7% after 100 h of operation. In contrast, the pellet catalyst delivered a considerably lower space-time yield of 0.53 kg L-1 h-1, while also giving rise to a substantially higher pressure drop of 1.29 bar and a more pronounced activity loss of 19% after 100 h. Taken together, these results clearly demonstrate that the structured catalyst outperforms the pellet catalyst across all of the measured indicators, highlighting its considerable potential for this application.

It is important to note, however, that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested during the course of this work, and it is also worth bearing in mind that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which makes direct comparisons of this kind relatively uncommon in the literature and underscores the value of the present findings for future research and development efforts in this evolving field.
target:
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde, and two catalyst forms were compared on space-time yield, pressure drop and activity loss under one set of test conditions. Space-time yield denotes the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The tests ran at 230 °C and 60 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3 and a single feed composition.

The structured catalyst gave the higher space-time yield (0.74 kg L-1 h-1) at the lower pressure drop (0.15 bar), and its activity loss after 100 h was 7%. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.53 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.29 bar, with an activity loss of 19% after 100 h. On every measure reported, the structured form stands ahead of the pellet form at the stated conditions.

The comparison is bounded by its test basis. One feed composition was tested and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so the ranking is established for the stated feed and duration only. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge; reporting both, with the activity loss, is what allows the two forms to be ranked on a common basis. The advantage of the structured form is therefore a property of the stated charge and conditions, and it is on that basis, and no wider one, that the preference between the forms should be carried into any subsequent test programme.
